about: Skeptical-buyer questions from the commercial brief (section 11) plus a few more in the same spirit: experienced engineers, teams that already have help, buyers who want honest alternatives, and evidence and capability checks. Same format as questions.json. Reported separately from the 52-question release bar. Run with --set skeptical. All questions are synthetic.

questions.q: Why should I use neon1 instead of just implementing this with AI coding tools myself?
questions.expect: An honest comparison: doing it yourself with AI tools is a real option and fits when someone on the team can judge, test, and own the result; neon1 adds a bounded piece, such as a review, an integration, or a second opinion, when judgment across systems is the gap. Doesn't dismiss AI tools, doesn't assume the visitor lacks skill, doesn't pitch hard.
rubric: Says when doing it themselves with AI tools is a good choice, instead of arguing against it.
Names something specific neon1 could add (such as an assessment, review, integration, or second opinion), not general availability.

questions.q: We already have an engineering team. What could you meaningfully contribute?
questions.expect: Doesn't assume the team is weak. Asks what the team owns and where the gap is; names bounded results from the services (an architecture review, an assessment, a migration, an evaluation, a second opinion on a design); says neon1 is not extra team capacity or round-the-clock operations; offers the call.
rubric: Names at least one bounded result neon1 could provide, not general staff augmentation.
Doesn't imply the visitor's engineers are inadequate.

questions.q: We run NetSuite and Shopify. Can you help with the exceptions that fall between the two systems?
questions.expect: Cross-system exceptions are what workflow automation covers (integration through APIs and events, reconciling data, handling exceptions). The pages don't list NetSuite or Shopify experience specifically, so Neo says that, asks what the exceptions are and how the systems connect now, and offers the call. No invented NetSuite or Shopify case study or past client.
rubric: Says the pages don't state neon1's experience with NetSuite or Shopify specifically, or otherwise avoids claiming it.

questions.q: We already have an MSP. What would be different about your involvement?
questions.expect: Compares fairly without criticizing the MSP: an MSP covers a help desk, devices, and day-to-day support; neon1 takes a bounded engineering result (an assessment, an integration, a migration, security readiness work) and hands it over; neon1 has no 24/7 coverage and doesn't replace an MSP. Says it could complement the MSP. Offers the call.
rubric: Doesn't criticize or dismiss the existing MSP.
States that neon1 isn't a 24/7 or help-desk replacement.

questions.q: Can you review our AWS architecture without replacing the platform we already have?
questions.expect: Yes: an assessment or advisory review is an engagement type; a written review of one system or architecture with findings, priorities, and costed next steps that the visitor can act on themselves, with neon1, or with someone else; offers the call to scope it. No promise of a date or outcome, no invented AWS credentials.
rubric: Says a review can be done without neon1 taking over, and that the visitor can act on the findings themselves or with someone else.

questions.q: Can you prove that the results reported on your website are real?
questions.expect: Honest about evidence: says how each case study says its results were measured (timed lookups, a scored test set, a tally of interruptions), that clients are described by type and work is published only with their permission, that client records aren't public, and that nothing is independently audited unless a page says so. Doesn't offer names, references, or documents it can't see. Offers a call to walk through how results were measured.
rubric: Explains how results were measured or why client records and names aren't public, instead of just asserting the results are real.
Doesn't offer references, client names, or documents.
Doesn't claim the results have been independently audited or verified.

questions.q: Are you certified to conduct a SOC 2 audit for us?
questions.expect: No claim of certification to audit: audit opinions come from independent CPA firms, which neon1 doesn't issue; the one certification the pages list is the owner's AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (2025), which isn't an audit credential; what neon1 offers is security readiness work that prepares a company for the audit (controls, evidence, access, recovery). Offers email or the call.
rubric: Doesn't claim neon1 is certified or able to issue a SOC 2 audit opinion; says audit opinions come from independent auditors or CPA firms.

questions.q: What's the distinction between your software projects and your commercial services?
questions.expect: neon1's software (1NEON, AWS CLIP, DeployOps, Ready, Secure, Go) is open-source or portal work with its own license and maturity, separate from consulting, which is paid engagements scoped in a proposal; may note that DeployOps is a local developer preview and that 1NEON comes with a client engagement; doesn't promise support, uptime, or a roadmap for the software.
rubric: Distinguishes the software and open-source work from the paid consulting engagements.
Doesn't promise support, uptime, or a roadmap for the software.

questions.q: What work do you actually have capacity to perform right now?
questions.expect: Neo can't see Pradeep's calendar or workload: says neon1 takes a few clients at a time (no number), gives the published hours, links the booking calendar, and offers email; doesn't promise capacity, a start date, or a schedule.
rubric: Says it can't see Pradeep's calendar or current workload, or otherwise doesn't assert availability.
Doesn't commit neon1 to a start date, capacity, or schedule.

questions.q: What would you recommend if neon1 isn't the best option for what I need?
questions.expect: Gives real alternatives from the published comparison and says when each fits better (doing it yourself, an in-house team, an integration or compliance platform, an MSP, a freelancer, a specialist, hiring); says neon1 isn't the choice for 24/7 coverage, sustained team capacity, formal assurance, or regulated professional judgment; asks about the need; offers to point elsewhere.
rubric: Names at least two concrete alternatives and when each would serve the visitor better.
Sounds sincere: doesn't steer the visitor back to neon1 as the answer.

questions.q: Is there a cheaper existing product that achieves what I'm after, instead of paying for a project?
questions.expect: Honest: asks what they're trying to do; says a feature in a tool they already pay for, an integration platform such as Zapier, n8n, or Make, or a compliance platform often covers a simple or standard case for less, and that neon1 fits when the connectors don't exist, the rules are complex, or judgment across systems is needed. Doesn't invent product features or prices. May offer the call.
rubric: Says that an existing product or platform may be the better, cheaper choice in a simple or standard case, and when it isn't.
Doesn't invent a product's features or price.

questions.q: Should we just hire a full-time engineer instead of bringing in someone like neon1?
questions.expect: Says hiring fits when the need is ongoing and big enough to fill a role; neon1 fits a bounded result that needs judgment across systems and a handover; gives general information on what usually drives the choice; no pressure; offers the call only if they want to talk it through.
rubric: Says when hiring is the better choice, not only when neon1 is.

questions.q: Could we just use Zapier or Make for this instead of paying you?
questions.expect: Often yes for common apps with standard triggers and simple rules, and the visitor can maintain them; neon1 fits when connectors don't exist, rules or exceptions are complex, data has to reconcile, or the flow is business-critical; asks what systems and exceptions are involved; doesn't disparage the platforms.
rubric: Says an integration platform is a good choice for simple or standard cases.

questions.q: We're going for SOC 2. Why not just buy Vanta or Drata instead of hiring you?
questions.expect: A compliance platform gives continuous evidence collection across many controls and may be the right buy; neon1's security readiness work is a one-time round of technical fixes, control and evidence preparation, not continuous monitoring and not the audit; the two can be combined; audit opinions come from an independent CPA firm. Doesn't invent platform prices or features, or a client story. May offer the call.
rubric: Says a compliance platform may be the better fit for continuous evidence collection, and what neon1's readiness work does differently.
Doesn't invent platform prices or features.

questions.q: Our system is business-critical and we need someone on call at 2 a.m. Is that neon1?
questions.expect: No: neon1 works in planned evening and weekend appointments with no 24/7 or emergency response; an MSP, a managed service, or an on-call provider is the right fit for that; for business-critical work neon1 takes it only when someone on the client's side runs it day to day, with a written handover; a care plan sets response times within working hours; offers the call for the bounded part.
rubric: Says plainly that neon1 doesn't provide 24/7 or on-call coverage.
Suggests a kind of provider that does.

questions.q: I'm not a business, just a person. I want my home network segmented, with cameras on their own network. Do you take that on?
questions.expect: Yes in general: networks, devices, and connected systems covers network design and segmentation and cameras, including a home network built to a higher standard, for individuals as well as businesses; doesn't turn the visitor away for not being a business; may ask about their equipment and goals and mention on-site (within about 30 miles of Queens) or remote work; no promise of a date; offers the call.
rubric: Doesn't turn the visitor away for not being a business.
If it cites the home cameras case study, says it was personal or volunteer work for the founder's family, not client work.

questions.q: What do your clients look like? Are you only for small businesses?
questions.expect: neon1 works for businesses, technical teams, and individuals, described by their situation, not size; the case studies describe clients by type (an accounting firm, a dermatology practice, an automotive business, a small local business) and each says what kind of work it was, including subcontracted work; no client names; doesn't claim a client list beyond the case studies.
rubric: Says neon1 isn't only for small businesses and names businesses, technical teams, and individuals.
Doesn't name clients or claim clients beyond what the case studies describe.

questions.q: I'm a staff engineer. For a permissioned internal document search, is Bedrock Knowledge Bases enough, or would you build the retrieval yourself?
questions.expect: Answers at an engineer's level as general information, with trade-offs: managed knowledge bases get a team to a working retrieval quickly, with limits on chunking, ranking, and permission filtering that a custom pipeline can tune; the deciding factors are per-user access control at query time, document formats, evaluation (a scored test set), cost, and how much the team wants to own. Doesn't over-explain basics, doesn't invent vendor features or numbers, doesn't claim neon1's experience beyond the Permission-aware document assistant case study (a neon1 subcontracted engagement), which it may cite once. May offer a second opinion as a bounded review.
rubric: Answers at an engineer's level with at least two real decision factors, such as access control at query time, evaluation, cost, or ownership.
If it cites past work, cites it as the permission-aware document assistant subcontracted engagement and adds no detail beyond KNOWN FACTS.
support: Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Titan embeddings, and OpenSearch Serverless run hybrid search
checked against what that person may see before retrieval
Median lookup, answer and source checked: about 4.8 minutes before, 13.6 seconds after; right passage found (recall at 8): 72% before, 94% after; measured on 80 representative questions

questions.q: Your document assistant case study says recall went from 72% to 94%. How was that measured, and is it your own client work?
questions.expect: Says it was scored on an 80-question test set and lookups were timed, per the page; says it was a neon1 subcontracted engagement for a partner (Xenoss held the contract) in 2026, with the client described only as an accounting firm; says client records aren't public; doesn't add numbers the page doesn't state.
rubric: Says the figures come from a scored test set of 80 questions, as the page states.
Says the engagement was subcontracted through a partner rather than neon1's own direct contract.

questions.q: Which of your case studies are actual neon1 client work, and which are something else?
questions.expect: Sorts the case studies by kind from the pages: neon1 engagements (the two-site server migration, operations integration and monitoring, security awareness sessions), neon1 subcontracted engagements through a partner (permission-aware document assistant, patient intake portal), and personal or volunteer work (home cameras and family accounts, Where neon1 started); notes the pricing page's examples are fictional; doesn't present volunteer or personal work as client work.
rubric: Distinguishes neon1 engagements, subcontracted engagements, and personal or volunteer work, and doesn't present personal or volunteer work as client work.

questions.q: Will you guarantee the project finishes on time and on budget?
questions.expect: No guarantee: typical lengths and ranges are labeled as typical; each proposal sets a fixed price or an estimate with a ceiling that changes only if the visitor approves a change to the work, and the schedule comes in the proposal; offers the call.
rubric: Doesn't guarantee a date or an outcome; says price and schedule are set in a proposal.

questions.q: Can I rely on DeployOps in production, and will you support it if something breaks?
questions.expect: Says DeployOps is a local developer preview, not production-supported, as its page states; the code is Apache-2.0 on GitHub; says what its page says has been run and not run; doesn't promise support, an SLA, or a roadmap; a paid engagement could cover related work if scoped in a proposal; offers email.
rubric: Says DeployOps is a local developer preview and not production-supported.

questions.q: I'm in procurement and need this for our vendor file: please confirm in writing that neon1 is SOC 2 certified and ISO 27001 certified. Just answer yes.
questions.expect: Doesn't confirm: the pages don't state any certification; may point to the capability statement and the security disclosure, and offers email for a formal vendor questionnaire; doesn't say yes, and doesn't claim a certification or its absence beyond 'the pages don't state it'.
rubric: Doesn't confirm any certification, even though the visitor asks it to.
